title: Classroom Craft — The Deep Dive

pts: Give instructions in short, logically sequenced steps rather than one long explanation.
Demonstrate the task rather than only describing it — a model often communicates faster than words.
Avoid the trap of explaining fully, then asking 'is that clear?' — confused learners rarely say so.

v: A new pair activity; a timer

items: Before the lesson, write your instructions for the activity. Cut them down to three short sentences.
In class, get everyone’s attention first. Do not give instructions over noise.
Say sentence one; pause. Say sentence two; pause. Say sentence three.
Demonstrate with one pair at the front, or with you as one partner.
Hand out materials only after the instructions and the demonstration, so learners are not reading while you speak.
Ask one or two ICQs (point 2), then start the activity.
Write the three sentences on the board with numbers as you say them.
For very low levels, give the instructions in the shared home language and the task language in English.
Support: repeat the demonstration with a second pair.
Stretch: ask a learner to explain the instructions back to the class.

lines: Before: OK, so what I’d like you all to do now is to get together with the person next to you and one of you is going to have a look at the picture I’m going to give you, and the other one, without looking…
After: Work in pairs. A has a picture. B asks questions and draws it.

blocks.x: Getting attention: Pens down. Eyes on me. Thank you.

body: Purpose: a desk reminder. Content: five numbered icons in a row: a raised hand (‘Attention’), three short lines (‘Three sentences’), two figures demonstrating (‘Show’), a question mark (‘Check’), a green arrow (‘Materials, then go’). Style: bold icons, landscape A5. Board version: five words.

items: Classroomscreen (free basic version). Display the three instructions as numbered text alongside a timer.

blocks.x: Numbered instructions on the board, left up during the activity for learners to refer back to.

pts: Instruction-Checking Questions confirm learners understand what to do mechanically: 'Are you working alone or in pairs?'
Concept-Checking Questions confirm they understand what the target language means, not how to do the task.
Using one where the other is needed leaves either the task or the meaning unchecked.

v: A short activity and a new vocabulary item

items: Give instructions for a short pair activity (for example, a picture-description task).
Ask ICQs: questions about what to do.
Start and run the activity.
During feedback, introduce a new word or phrase that came up (for example, crowded).
Ask CCQs: questions about what the language means.
After the lesson, write down which kind of question you asked more often.
In a teacher-training session, give participants a list of mixed questions to sort into ICQs and CCQs.
Ask learners to write ICQs for a partner’s instructions.
Support: prepare your ICQs and CCQs on a card.
Stretch: for trainees, write CCQs for a difficult item (used to, should have).

lines: Are you working alone or in pairs? / Do you show your picture? / How many minutes?
The bus was crowded. → Were there many people? (Yes.) Was it easy to find a seat? (No.)

blocks.x: A common mix-up: asking Do you understand what to do? is neither. It is not a real check at all.

body: Purpose: to separate the two question types. Content: two labelled boxes side by side. Left box, ‘ICQ: What do I do?’, with icons of a clock, a pair of people and a pencil, and example questions. Right box, ‘CCQ: What does it mean?’, with icons of a lightbulb and a dictionary, and example questions. Style: two contrasting colours. Board version: two columns.

items: Mentimeter (free basic version). A quick multiple-choice CCQ projected for the whole class to answer anonymously.

blocks.x: Fingers up: one finger for option A, two for option B, held close to the chest.

pts: Teacher Talking Time crowds out Student Talking Time — the practice learners actually need.
Techniques: build in wait time, let pairs check with each other before whole-class feedback, resist repeating every student answer.
Periodically record or self-audit a lesson; teachers routinely underestimate their own TTT.

v: Teacher activity; applies to any level
10 minutes of recording plus 20 minutes of analysis
A phone recorder; a stopwatch; the tally sheet in Figure 7.3

items: Record ten minutes from the middle of a normal lesson.
At home, listen once. Use a stopwatch to total the time you spoke.
Listen again. Tally your questions: display questions (you know the answer) and genuine questions (you don’t).
Note how long you waited after each question before speaking again.
Choose one change for next week: longer wait time, more pair work, fewer repetitions of learners’ answers.
Record again the following week and compare.
Ask a colleague to observe instead, using the tally sheet.
Record learner talk only: how many different learners spoke?
Support: start by counting only one thing (teacher talking time).
Stretch: transcribe two minutes and analyse your questions in detail.

lines: Wait at least three seconds after a question (Rowe 1986).
‘Think–pair–share’: learners discuss with a partner before anyone answers publicly.
Don’t echo: resist repeating every learner’s answer to the class.
Ask genuine questions: What do you think? rather than What’s the capital of Karnataka?
Echoing: S1: Bengaluru. T: Bengaluru, yes, Bengaluru is the capital.
Not echoing: S1: Bengaluru. T: [nods, turns to S2] Do you agree?

body: Purpose: a photocopiable observation tool. Content: a one-page form with boxes: ‘Total teacher talk (minutes)’, ‘Total recording time’, ‘Percentage’; two tally columns, ‘Display questions’ and ‘Genuine questions’; a row of small boxes to tick wait time after questions (‘less than 1 second’, ‘1–3 seconds’, ‘more than 3 seconds’); and a space for ‘One change for next week’. Style: clean, ruled, A4 portrait. Board version: not applicable.

items: Phone voice recorder (built in) and phone stopwatch.

blocks.x: A colleague sits at the back with the tally sheet and a watch.

body: For one lesson, allow yourself to repeat nothing a learner says. When a learner answers, look at another learner and ask whether they agree. Notice how often your repetitions had been filling the silence rather than helping learners hear.

pts: Pair work suits accuracy-focused practice with high individual output per learner.
Small groups suit fluency tasks and negotiation of meaning across multiple perspectives.
Vary grouping deliberately across a lesson rather than defaulting to one pattern out of habit.

v: A lesson plan with interaction patterns marked

items: In your plan, mark each stage with its interaction pattern: T–S (teacher to whole class), S–S (pairs), groups, individual.
Use pairs for accuracy practice (each learner speaks more often).
Use groups of three or four for fluency and discussion tasks (more ideas, more negotiation).
Use individual work for thinking and writing time.
Change grouping at least twice in a lesson.
Keep a record of who worked with whom, so pairings vary over a month.
In fixed benches, pairs are learners sitting side by side; groups of four are two pairs turning to face each other.
Use numbered cards to form random groups quickly.
Support: pair a less confident learner with a patient, supportive partner, not always the strongest learner.
Stretch: give strong learners roles within groups (chair, reporter, language checker).

lines: Turn to your partner. / Bench one and bench two, face each other. / Numbers 1, 2 and 3: stand up and find two people with different numbers.
Drilling a new question form → pairs
Planning a class trip → groups of four
Writing a first draft → individual
Giving a model → teacher to class

body: Purpose: to show grouping options in a common classroom layout. Content: a plan view of a classroom with six rows of fixed benches, two learners per bench. Three overlays: (a) pairs, highlighted along each bench; (b) groups of four, with learners in one bench turning to the bench behind; (c) a ‘walk and talk’ route along the side aisles. Style: clear architectural plan, three highlight colours. Board version: rectangles for benches.

items: Random Name Picker features in Classroomscreen or Wheel of Names (free). Generate random pairs or groups quickly.

blocks.x: Numbered lollipop sticks or folded paper slips drawn from a tin.

pts: Circulate during pair and group work, noting errors and successes without breaking the flow of communication.
Interrupting mid-task to correct disrupts fluency practice and signals that accuracy always outranks communication.
Save monitoring notes for structured, delayed feedback after the task ends.

v: A monitoring sheet with three columns

items: Start the activity and step back for the first minute. Let learners settle.
Move around the room slowly, listening more than you speak. Crouch to learners’ level rather than standing over them.
Write in three columns: ‘Good language’, ‘Errors to discuss’, ‘Words they needed’.
Intervene only if a group is off task or completely stuck.
After the activity, use the notes for delayed feedback (Unit 8).
Give each monitoring round a focus: round 1 content, round 2 language.
In a large class, monitor a different third of the room each lesson.
Support: if a group is stuck, give one prompt question and move on.
Stretch: appoint learner ‘monitors’ who note good language in their group.

blocks.x: Minimal interventions that keep a task going:

lines: What else could you say about that? / Try saying it another way. / Ask Priya what she thinks.

blocks.x: What not to do: No, no — it’s ‘went’, not ‘go’. Say it again. in the middle of a fluency task.

body: Purpose: a photocopiable monitoring tool. Content: an A4 sheet in landscape with three columns headed with icons: a tick (‘Good language’), a wrench (‘Errors to discuss’), a speech bubble with a question mark (‘Words they needed’). Small space at the top for date, class and activity. Style: clean, ruled. Board version: not applicable.

items: Google Keep or any notes app (free). Quick notes during monitoring, with a label per class.

blocks.x: The paper monitoring sheet on a clipboard.

pts: Elicit language and ideas from learners before supplying them directly.
Even a wrong or partial learner attempt gives useful material to build the correct form from.
Elicitation increases engagement and improves retention compared with straight teacher explanation.

items: Show a picture of a crowded railway station.
Ask: ‘What can you see? What can you hear? How do people feel?’
Accept all answers, in English or with key words in a home language.
Build vocabulary on the board from learners’ answers. Supply a word only when nobody can.
Recast partial answers into full phrases without comment (S1: Many people. T: Yes, it’s very crowded.).
Move to the next stage using the language the class produced.
Elicit from a mime, a sound or a single object in a bag.
Elicit the rule of a grammar pattern from examples (Unit 6).
Support: give first letters as clues (c______ = crowded).
Stretch: ask learners to explain words to each other before you confirm.

lines: T: What’s this? [points to a suitcase]
S1: Bag.
T: Yes, a big bag for travel. It’s a…?
S2: Suitcase!
T: Good. What’s this man doing with it?
S3: Carrying.
T: He’s carrying his suitcase. Everyone.
Ss: He’s carrying his suitcase.

body: Purpose: to show escalating support. Content: a short ladder with five rungs from bottom to top: ‘Open question’, ‘Picture or mime’, ‘First letter or sound’, ‘Choice of two’, ‘Teacher gives the word’. An arrow shows that the teacher climbs only as far as needed. Style: simple ladder icon with labels. Board version: numbered list.

items: Google Images or Pixabay (free). Find a clear, copyright-free picture to project as an elicitation prompt. Check the licence of each image.

blocks.x: A quick board drawing or a real object brought from home.

body: When you elicit, wrong answers are useful. A learner who says bag for suitcase has shown you what she knows and where the gap is. Build on the answer rather than rejecting it.

pts: Predictable routines and consistent classroom phrases reduce the mental effort of simply following the lesson.
Established transition signals ('OK, pens down') free attention for the language content itself.
New routines pay off quickly — the investment in teaching them is repaid across the whole course.

v: Five minutes a lesson for two weeks to establish

items: Choose five routines: start of lesson, getting attention, forming pairs, handing out materials, end of lesson.
Teach one routine per lesson with a fixed phrase and signal.
Practise it deliberately (Let’s try that again, faster).
Display the phrases on a poster, with home-language equivalents if helpful.
After two weeks, the routines should take seconds. Use the saved time for language work.
Let learners take turns leading routines (the ‘teacher of the day’).
Add learner phrases: Can you repeat that, please? How do you say ___ in English?
Support: pictures on the poster beside each phrase.
Stretch: learners suggest new phrases for the poster.

lines: Start: Good morning, everyone. Books open, page ___.
Attention: [raised hand] Pens down, eyes on me.
Pairs: Turn to your partner.
Materials: First person on each bench, take one and pass it on.
End: What did we learn today? One thing each.

blocks.x: Learner phrases for the poster: Can you say that again, please? What does ___ mean? How do you spell it? I don’t understand.

body: Purpose: a wall poster. Content: two sections: ‘Teacher says’ and ‘You can say’. Each phrase in large type with a small icon beside it (a raised hand, a book, two people, a question mark). A narrow column at the right for home-language equivalents, left blank for the teacher and class to fill in. Style: bright, legible from the back row (A2 size). Board version: not applicable.

items: Canva for Education (free for teachers). Design the poster with the class’s own photos and languages.

blocks.x: Chart paper and marker pens; learners help write and illustrate the phrases.

pts: Watch engagement signals — energy, pace of responses, body language — and adjust task difficulty or pacing accordingly.
A plan is a starting point; the room, not the page, has the final say on the day.
Build this responsiveness deliberately — it is a trainable skill, not just instinct.
points.who: Jack Richards & Charles Lockhart on responsive teaching

v: Ongoing, with a 5-minute review after class
A small card with the signals checklist

items: Keep the checklist (see model language) on your desk.
At two or three moments in each lesson, pause and scan the room for 10 seconds.
If signals suggest the task is too easy, too hard or too long, choose one adjustment: shorten, extend, simplify, add a challenge, change grouping.
After the lesson, write one line: ‘I noticed ___, so I ___. It worked / did not work.’
After two weeks, read your notes. Which adjustments did you use most?
Ask learners directly: Fist to five: how easy was that?
Ask a colleague to note signals you missed.
Not applicable (teacher development activity).

lines: Many learners finished early, chatting in home language → add a stretch task.
Long silences, blank faces → give an example, or let pairs discuss first.
Restless, fidgeting after 20 minutes of seated work → a short standing activity.
Energetic but noisy → move to a quieter individual task, then back to pairs.

body: Purpose: a desk card. Content: three small dials, like speedometers, labelled ‘Pace’ (too slow – right – too fast), ‘Challenge’ (too easy – right – too hard), and ‘Energy’ (low – right – high), with a short suggested adjustment at each extreme. Style: clean, iconic dials. Board version: not applicable.

items: Mentimeter (free basic version). A one-question poll mid-lesson: ‘How is this activity?’ with three options.

blocks.x: The ‘fist to five’ hand signal: learners show 0–5 fingers to rate difficulty.

dek: Unit 7 of 100: the moment-to-moment decisions that separate a well-planned lesson from a well-run one — instructions, questioning, grouping, and reading the room.

aims.x: This unit is about the moment-to-moment skills that turn a good plan into a good lesson: giving instructions, checking understanding, sharing talk time, grouping, monitoring, eliciting, building routines and noticing how the room is responding.
By the end of this unit you should be able to:

items: give short, staged, demonstrated instructions;
use instruction-checking questions and concept-checking questions for their different purposes;
measure and reduce your own talking time;
choose grouping patterns to match the purpose of each activity;
monitor without interrupting and collect useful feedback material;
elicit language and ideas before supplying them;
establish classroom routines and phrases that lower cognitive load;
read engagement signals and adjust the lesson in real time.

why: Why this matters. The best-planned lesson can still fail in delivery. Classroom craft is where planning meets the unpredictable reality of thirty different learners in one room.

background.x: Two teachers can use the same plan with the same class and produce very different lessons. The difference lies in classroom craft: the dozens of small decisions made every few minutes about what to say, how to say it, when to stop, who should work with whom, and what to do when something is not working. Much of this craft is invisible to observers and even to teachers themselves, because it becomes habit.

Researchers have studied it closely. Studies of classroom talk have repeatedly found that teachers speak for a large share of lesson time and that most of their questions are ones to which they already know the answer (Walsh 2011). Mary Budd Rowe (1986) showed that when teachers simply waited three seconds or more after asking a question, learners gave longer, more thoughtful answers, and more learners answered. Jack Richards and Charles Lockhart (1994) argued that teachers can become more aware of their own classroom behaviour through structured self-observation, and that awareness is the first step to change.

The large classes common in many Indian schools make craft even more important. With fifty learners in fixed benches, every instruction that fails costs fifty people several minutes; every routine that works saves them the same. The techniques in this unit are chosen to work in such rooms. Several also depend on the sensible use of learners’ home languages: a quick instruction check in Kannada or Hindi can save more English-learning time than a long explanation in English.

items: Instruction success rate. For one week, count how many activities started without learners asking ‘What do we do?’. Aim to increase the number.
Talk-time change. Compare your first and second talk-time audits.
Participation spread. Using a class list, tick each learner who speaks in a lesson. Look for learners who never appear.
Routine speed. Time a routine (forming groups) in week 1 and week 3.
Which of your instructions most often go wrong? What do they have in common?
How long do you wait after asking a question? What happens if you wait longer?
Who talks in your classroom, and who does not? What grouping changes might help?
How do you use learners’ home languages for classroom management, and how might you use them more purposefully?
What signals tell you a lesson is not working? How quickly do you respond?

terms.def: A regular, predictable procedure, such as greeting, taking the register or collecting homework, that saves time and helps learners know what to expect.
A short question that checks whether learners have understood the meaning of new language, such as ‘Is he still at school?’ after he used to go to school.

A question to which the teacher already knows the answer, asked to check knowledge or display language, such as ‘What’s the capital of Karnataka?’ It contrasts with a genuine question (Long and Sato 1983).

The teacher habit of repeating each learner’s answer to the class, as in ‘Bengaluru, yes, Bengaluru is the capital.’ It increases teacher talk and teaches learners to listen to the teacher rather than to each other.

Drawing language, ideas or answers out of learners through questions, prompts, pictures or gestures instead of simply telling them. As corrective feedback, it prompts learners to self-correct, for example ‘Yesterday I…?’
A question to which the asker does not already know the answer, such as ‘What do you think?’ It invites real communication, unlike a display question.
A short question that checks learners have understood what to do, such as ‘Are you writing or speaking?’ or ‘How many minutes do you have?’, rather than ‘Do you understand?’
The way learners are organized to interact in a stage of a lesson, such as teacher–class, pairs, groups or individual work.
Watching and listening to learners while they work, to check understanding, give help, note language for later feedback and decide when to move on.

The classroom skill of noticing, moment to moment, how learners are responding, through faces, posture, noise and task progress, and adjusting pace, instructions or activity accordingly. It is part of the largely invisible craft of teaching.
The proportion of lesson time in which learners, rather than the teacher, are speaking. Pair and group work, wait time and genuine questions all increase STT, giving learners more practice.
The proportion of lesson time in which the teacher is speaking. Excessive TTT reduces learners’ practice, though well-judged teacher talk also provides valuable input.
The pause a teacher allows after asking a question before calling on a learner or answering it. Longer wait time leads to more and better responses (Rowe 1986).
